reflections.body: Opening night behind us. Forty covers, the pass never cooled. Salt, smoke, the tick of tickets. I remade the branzino three times before it went out — skin not crisp enough, then too dark, then right. Nobody at the table knows how close it came to being wrong. My hands know.

Saturday double. The line moves like one animal when it's good, and tonight it was good. I don't stop, I don't sit. If I sit somebody sees me not moving and thinks the new place is soft. Ribeye rested four minutes, plated at 51 degrees at the center, exact. A review came in. Four stars. I read the one thing they didn't love five times.

01:40. Todos se fueron. La cocina apagada menos la luz del pase. Hice el arroz de coco como lo hacía mi abuela, con la letra de ella al lado, la receta manchada. Lo emplaté igualito. Igualito. Y me quedé ahí parado y no pude respirar bien. No sé por qué lloré. Se me salió y ya. La cocina huele a ella. No escribo más.

They clapped again tonight. A regular grabbed my arm, said this is the best food in Orlando. I smiled, said gracias, and went back to check the walk-in temps. Everybody claps and I'm back there waiting for the night it all comes apart. One bad service. That's all it takes for them to see.

My father called cooking women's work. Thirty years and he never once put a fork to anything I made. I plated a dish tonight I know he would have — no. He wouldn't have. He never. Yo cocinaba y él ni volteaba la cara. Ni una vez probó. Ni una. No quiero escribir más de esto ahorita.

Putting a new plate on the menu next week — patacón with lime crema and a little dish of the sea, the way Barranquilla tastes in February. I want to name it after the city. Sabor a Barranquilla. Feels like too much of me on a menu card, but Diego said name it and let people meet you. First time in weeks I felt something that wasn't fear when I read my own handwriting.

messages.body: Is it normal to not feel the good stuff? People love the place. I just feel the next service coming at me.
Very normal, Marcos — and worth noticing that the fear talks louder than any clap. We don't have to fix that yet. Just keep writing it down like you're doing. The noticing is the work.
Naming the new dish after Barranquilla. Nervous to put that much of me on paper but I'm doing it.

notes.body: First weeks: entries are almost all sensory — heat, salt, the pass. He keeps the lens on the food and off himself. The 'remake it three times' pattern is right there in the branzino. He names perfectionism and his abuela's recipes as his own; hasn't yet connected the perfectionism to a fear of being found out. Not mine to name yet either.

The late-night arroz de coco entry — plating his abuela's recipe exactly, crying at the pass, and stopping himself ('no escribo más'). This is tender and unfinished. Do NOT probe. He set it down himself; my job is to let him know it was received, not to open it. Language shifted fully to Spanish here — where English stops holding, the truth arrives.

The father entry broke mid-thought into Spanish and closed with 'no quiero escribir más ahorita.' Hold the space, no follow-up question. The not-enoughness clearly roots here — cooking as the one place he could be somebody, and the man who called it 'women's work' never tasting a bite. He's circling it, not ready to land. Let him circle.

The Barranquilla dish is the first opening that's safe to deepen — lighter, forward-facing, mood up, and Diego's encouragement already in the frame. A gentle question here about what it feels like to sign his own name to a plate could invite the connection between his worth and the last review, without forcing it. This is where the Rewiring Self-Worth thread can quietly start.
